abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model’s developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk–coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by $-8.4$ and $+5.6$ points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

sections.body: Typed-decision models score options that callers supply at request time, so accuracy depends on label wording the model's developer does not control. The section cites prior work showing that prompt-based models are far more sensitive to target words than to the instruction (Webson and Pavlick, 2022), that label words are searched because the choice matters (Gao et al., 2021), and that training on label descriptions improves handling of verbalizer changes (Gao et al., 2023). The question is which unfamiliar label wordings a model handles better when training presents each label in several surface forms. The stated contributions are a controlled measurement over ten label vocabularies, a finding on augmentation, out-of-distribution results against an open model, and four hazards in comparing releases.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Label wording set at request time shapes accuracy, so the paper tests whether augmented training helps unfamiliar labels.

sections.body: Ru-Jev is a pointwise cross-encoder: each context-option pair is scored independently, and the scores are normalised across options with a single scalar temperature fitted after training. Training uses cross-entropy over the options of each example. Two consequences follow. The output does not depend on option order, because no option sees another. The distribution over any subset of a candidate set is obtained exactly by renormalising that subset's scores, so the same probe can be evaluated at five and at eighteen candidates from one scoring pass. The cost is linear in the number of options, unlike models that read all options in one pass.
sections.heading: Typed decisions
sections.headline: Each option is scored independently, so one scoring pass gives exact distributions over any candidate subset.

sections.body: The encoder is mmBERT-base, and training uses thirteen tasks built from open Russian-language datasets, including RussianSuperGLUE, RuCoLA, MERA reasoning sets, ruMTEB classification tasks, MASSIVE and a toxicity set. The mix contains 143,991 training and 26,746 validation decisions. Training ran four epochs. The fourth overfits: training loss falls to 0.085 while validation loss rises to 0.820. A temperature fitted on its outputs reaches 3.92, against 1.864 for the released third epoch. Epoch selection and temperature fitting both used the validation split, which includes MASSIVE validation rows. The datasets used in the later out-of-distribution section played no role in model selection.
sections.heading: Model and data
sections.headline: Ru-Jev, a 307M-parameter cross-encoder, is trained on thirteen Russian tasks and releases its third epoch.

sections.body: Release v1.1 presents each MASSIVE scenario label as its English key and as an ordinary Russian word, and both forms occur for all 18 scenarios in the rebuilt training mix. Release v1.3 stores several surface forms per label and draws one uniformly per training example. Its forms include the English key, an ordinary Russian label, transliterations of the key for MASSIVE intents, five wordings for toxicity and for review sentiment, and four for review rating. The releases also differ in validation partitions, an intermediate release, and learning-rate schedules, because v1.1 was trained for three epochs and v1.3 for four. The authors therefore attribute differences to the release, and to the augmentation only where the probe design isolates it.
sections.heading: The two releases
sections.headline: Release v1.3 draws one of several label wordings per training example; v1.1 used fewer wordings and changed other data.

sections.body: All wording probes use the same 1,000 questions from the MASSIVE scenario validation split, with 7 duplicates, and each question has one gold label among 18. Five-candidate sets have chance 0.20 and eighteen-candidate sets have chance 0.056. Vocabularies were written during development, generated by rule, or written by a separate AI assistant session. Every probe label was checked against training options by exact equality and prefix in both directions, and slices remove overlapping gold labels. Statistics are exact McNemar tests and a two-stage bootstrap over labels and then questions, with Holm adjustment over 23 cells. A reading rule for one slang comparison was recorded before its score file was opened, but the authors do not call this pre-registration.
sections.heading: Evaluation design
sections.headline: Probes hold questions fixed and vary only label wording, scored at five and eighteen candidates with overlap checks.

sections.body: Table 2 compares the releases on identical questions, varying only label wording. On every held-out vocabulary made of words, v1.3 has the higher accuracy in both settings. English-derived jargon on the strict slice gains +0.235 with five candidates and +0.142 with eighteen. The paper reports that eleven of these fourteen gains survive the Holm correction. Office slang with eighteen candidates is a reshuffle, with 5 labels improving and 6 getting worse. On three-letter abbreviations v1.3 is not better, with -0.060 on the clean slice. On opaque codes, v1.1 is below chance and v1.3 at chance on the strict slice with eighteen candidates.
sections.heading: Which wordings the augmented release gains on
sections.headline: Augmented release is more accurate on held-out word vocabularies, but gives no usable gain on abbreviations or codes.

sections.body: Two Russian datasets were used by neither release: news headline topics with six classes and CEDR emotions with five classes. Table 3 gives accuracy of 0.652 for v1.1 and 0.568 for v1.3 on headlines, and 0.455 and 0.511 on emotions. Laya reaches 0.610 on headlines and 0.605 on emotions. Laya is markedly overconfident on headlines, with a confidence-minus-accuracy gap of +0.242, and not on emotions. Residual calibration error after each model refits its own temperature is 0.056 to 0.067 for Ru-Jev over 25 seeded splits. The authors make no claim of superiority over Laya in accuracy or calibration. The large card-bench gap is treated as home advantage, since the MASSIVE training split is in Ru-Jev's mix.
sections.heading: Unseen datasets and an open comparison model
sections.headline: On two unseen datasets, v1.3 is 8.4 points below v1.1 on headlines and 5.6 points above on emotions.

sections.body: On the six RussianSuperGLUE tasks, whose rows and option sets are identical in both builds, the releases answer 8,120 of 10,157 decisions correctly and disagree on 1,680, 840 in each direction (McNemar p=1.0). Over 25 random half-splits, v1.3 takes a lower temperature in every split, at 1.50–1.60 against 1.94–2.10, so its raw scores are less overconfident. Residual expected calibration error after each release receives its own temperature is 0.0190 against 0.0191. Table 6 shows Ru-Jev is 1.2 times slower than Laya with two options and 2.4 times slower with eighteen. The selective-prediction figures are optimistic, because the same split informed epoch selection.
sections.heading: In-distribution accuracy, calibration and cost
sections.headline: Both releases score 0.7994 on the six in-distribution tasks, and v1.3 needs a lower temperature.

sections.body: The first hazard is that validation carves shared one random stream, so adding a label style changed later partitions. 90.3% of new acceptability validation rows had been in v1.1 training data, and the apparent drop from 0.909 to 0.647 was v1.1 scored on its own training rows; on held-out rows it scores 0.650. The second is matching rows on input text alone, which allowed a toxicity gain of 0.722 to 0.954 that reflected option wording, since v1.1 scores 0.961 with the wording it trained on. The third is a summary of 0.7948 against 0.7920 on 5,078 decisions printed beside a table over 10,157. The fourth is a stale reference copy that produced seed runs without transliteration styles, with jargon accuracy of 0.588 and 0.611.
sections.heading: Four hazards in comparing releases
sections.headline: Four comparison hazards, including shared random streams and stale references, each produced a misleading result.

sections.body: Each release was trained once, and the released v1.3 has no valid second seed. Two v1.1 replicates scored 0.658 and 0.622 on jargon with five candidates, so the released baseline of 0.633 lies inside its own seed range of 0.036 on all labels and 0.046 on the clean slice. The text describes the jargon gains as roughly four to six times larger than that range, but seed variance was measured only for v1.1 on jargon with five candidates. The releases also differ in data partitions and toxicity wording, so out-of-distribution changes cannot be attributed to augmentation alone. Each style is one vocabulary of 18 labels, so style and vocabulary are confounded, and the model cannot report that no option fits.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Single training runs, confounded data changes, and seed variance comparable to several Table 2 differences limit the claims.

sections.body: The conclusion is that an evaluation which varies the model but not the label wording measures the easy case. The study found the augmented release more accurate on unfamiliar word labels, no usable gain on abbreviations or opaque codes, and that better accuracy does not by itself bring fewer confident errors when the candidate set is large. The practical steps are to choose augmentation styles that resemble the wording a deployment will use, to refit the temperature on that wording, and to evaluate on styles absent from the augmentation at more than one candidate-set size. The authors also recommend the release comparison protocol of Section 9.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Evaluations that vary only the model miss label-wording effects, so augmentation should match deployment wording and temperature be refitted.

sections.body: Weights of both releases are on Hugging Face under the name besktech/ru-jev, with v1.1 on a branch. Training code, the data builder, all label vocabularies, the overlap audit, the latency benchmark, per-row scores, the analysis script, the SHA-256 hashes of the weight files and the recorded split seed are in the GitHub repository beskvladimir-create/ru-jev. The release used for the paper, v1.3.0, is archived at Zenodo under doi:10.5281/zenodo.23986847. Code and weights are under the MIT licence. Training data keep their own licences, which are listed per source in the repository.
sections.heading: Data and code availability
sections.headline: Weights, code, vocabularies, per-row scores and a Zenodo archive of the release are available.
